gap: No result ChatGPT got that I could open states, in Apple's own words, that an iPhone cuts wireless charging speed while you run processor- or graphics-heavy apps or the camera, or while a wired accessory is plugged in, so a 25 W snap-on bank used on a phone in the hand will not hold 25 W; nor that the iPhone 16e and 17e are excluded from 25 W.
standout_why: I compared against Macworld (cited; first 100,000 of 123,900 characters read) and Anker's 'Best Qi2 25W' blog (rank 1). Macworld already states the core gate: 25 W only on iPhone 16 to 18 families on iOS 26 or later, older iPhones at 15 W, iPhone Air at 20 W. Anker's blog already states the thermal gate: output drops to 15 W past 104°F (40°C). Neither gives Apple's in-use and wired-accessory conditions, the 16e/17e exclusion, Anker's own statement that Android phones get 15 W from the MagGo 2 Pro, or that the certification logo reads 'Qi2 25W' rather than 'Qi2.2'. I could not open The Verge (cited; fetch blocked), TechRadar (cited; body came back truncated) or pickedtech (certificate error), so they may hold some of this.
decides: It confirms the picks only for a MagSafe iPhone 16 or later (not 16e/17e) on iOS 26 or later; there, all four candidates can negotiate 25 W. For an iPhone 15 or older, a 16e/17e, or (per Anker's own page for the MagGo 2 Pro) an Android phone, the bank delivers 15 W or less, so the 25 W premium buys nothing. Anker's fan is the only candidate feature aimed at the heat throttle, which makes the $109.99 MagGo 2 Pro defensible only for long 25 W sessions; that claim is Anker's own, with no test conditions given. For a phone used in the hand while charging, Apple's conditions mean the cheaper Baseus AM52 ($55.99) or INIU SnapGo ($44.99) lose little.

findings.label: Apple: what slows iPhone wireless charging
findings.value: "You might notice reduced charging speed if: You use graphics-intensive or processor-intensive apps, games, or features, including camera apps"; "For faster wireless charging, disconnect wired accessories from your iPhone."; "Your iPhone might put charging on hold temporarily" (temperature)
findings.source_title: About iPhone charge speeds - Apple Support
findings.note: Page published 2026-03-16. Quotes came through a page summariser, so re-check wording before publishing. The page gives no per-model wireless wattages. It also says to use "a MagSafe Charger or a Qi2-certified wireless charger" for faster wireless charging.

findings.label: WPC: name and promise of the 25 W standard
findings.value: "Qi v2.2.1, branded as Qi2 25W"; "delivering nearly 70% more charging power"; "can safely charge a smartphone battery from 0 to 50% in about 30 minutes"; "Only Qi Certified products can display the Qi or Qi2 logo"
findings.source_title: Qi Wireless Charging - Wireless Power Consortium
findings.note: 'Qi2.2' is the spec version; the consumer mark is 'Qi2 25W'. Arithmetic: 25 W / 15 W = 1.67, i.e. about 67% more than Qi2 15 W. The page does not say what happens when only one side is 25 W certified.

Google's own statement of which Pixels take 25 W. Search results say only the Pixel 10 Pro XL does and the Pixel 10 and 10 Pro stop at 15 W, which would conflict with Anker's 'Android phones will receive standard 15W'; the Google Store Pixelsnap page came back empty.
